title: Leicester Diwali Draws an Estimated 30,000 as Golden Mile Lights Up
excerpt: Leicester City Council said about 30,000 people attended Diwali Day on Sunday, November 8, 2026 — among the largest Diwali celebrations outside India, with the Philharmonia Orchestra and an Aakash Odedra Company finale at Cossington Street Recreation Ground.
body:
• Leicester's Diwali Day celebrations on Sunday, November 8, 2026 drew about 30,000 people, Leicester City Council said — an estimate, with City Mayor Sir Peter Soulsby describing the event as "enjoyed by an estimated 30,000 people."
  • The Golden Mile along Belgrave Road was illuminated, the Wheel of Light returned, and the main programme centred on Cossington Street Recreation Ground, with the Philharmonia Orchestra among the performers.
  • In a first for 2026, the Aakash Odedra Company led the stage finale, bringing together Bollywood dance from Shiamak, theatre from Red Lotus and music from the Philharmonia Orchestra.
  • Leicester's first public Diwali lights went up along Belgrave Road in 1983. The University of Leicester, an official sponsor this year, is also marking Diwali on campus this month with Rangoli making and Diya painting — full programme details are on the Visit Leicester Diwali page.

Leicester's Diwali celebrations attracted about 30,000 people to the city on Sunday, November 8, Leicester City Council said, in festivities described by the BBC as among the largest outside India. The Golden Mile along Belgrave Road was illuminated, the Wheel of Light returned to Belgrave Road, and venues across the city hosted exhibitions, workshops and family activities.

What the day looked like

The main focus of celebrations was Cossington Street Recreation Ground, where the Diwali Village and stage returned with food stalls, a family funfair and a community stage programme including a Puja ceremony led by the Leicester Hindu Festival Council, according to Leicester City Council. A full philharmonic orchestra — the Philharmonia Orchestra — was among the performers, the BBC reported. The council said the Aakash Odedra Company led the stage finale in a new production bringing together Bollywood dance from Shiamak, theatre from Red Lotus and music from the Philharmonia Orchestra, and that a suspended acrobat performance, Heliosphere, and a laser show closed the evening. Revellers travelled from as far away as Canada, the BBC reported, and city cleaners were out until late on Sunday night to clear the streets ahead of Monday's rush hour.

"Our Diwali celebrations are a hugely important part of Leicester's cultural calendar and attract visitors from all over the UK and beyond. We're very grateful to the University of Leicester for their sponsorship of this year's Diwali Day event, which was enjoyed by an estimated 30,000 people."

— Sir Peter Soulsby, Leicester City Mayor

A celebration built since 1983

Leicester's first public Diwali lights were displayed along Belgrave Road in 1983, the University of Leicester said, and the festival has since developed into a major celebration of the city's South Asian heritage. Today the celebrations encompass thousands of lights along Belgrave and Melton Roads alongside music, dance and cultural performances. The wider programme included community celebrations and performances at Attenborough Arts Centre, Leicester Cathedral, Haymarket Theatre, Curve and the Peepul Centre, and the Har Har Rangoli exhibition at Belgrave Neighbourhood Centre on November 7 and 8.

Leicester's connection with South Asia grew significantly in the second half of the 20th century as Indian communities settled in the city, including families arriving from East Africa; in the 1970s the city became home to many Asians expelled from Uganda. Professor Kamlesh Khunti of the University of Leicester, whose family originates from Gujarat and who grew up in Leicester's Highfields area, spoke at Sunday's celebrations. "In many ways, Leicester is a miniature version of India," he said. "People from across the Indian subcontinent have made Leicester their home, bringing with them different languages, faiths, traditions and cuisines."

Reading the 30,000 figure correctly

The headline number needs its qualifier: it is an estimate of attendance at a held event, not a count and not a pre-event projection. The BBC reported that Leicester City Council said about 30,000 people attended the celebration, and the City Mayor put it the same way — the Diwali Day event "was enjoyed by an estimated 30,000 people." Diwali, the festival of light, is celebrated by Hindu, Sikh and Jain communities and is associated with the triumph of light over darkness, good over evil and hope over despair. For the South Asian diaspora in Britain, Leicester's Diwali Day remains the country's flagship public celebration of the festival.
